reconcile.connective: Harmonizers read the "alone" of 1 Samuel as alone before the priest only: David's servants were waiting elsewhere and shared the bread.

discrepancy.connective: The objection that the Gospels err — David came to Ahimelech alone, so others could not have eaten the showbread with him — is pressed by Isaac of Troki, and is even preserved in the commentary Gill wrote to answer it.

skeptic.name: Isaac of Troki
skeptic.attribution: Isaac ben Abraham of Troki (d. 1594), Chizzuk Emunah / Faith Strengthened, Part 2, ch. 28 (1593)

excerpts.excerpt_text: though in Sa1 21:1 he is said to be "alone, and no man with him"; yet this must be understood either comparatively, having but very few with him, and which were as none, considering his dignity; or thus, though none came with him to Ahimelech … so that though no man was with him at the priest's house, yet there were some with him, and who partook with him in eating of the showbread.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly resolves the alone-vs-companions tension: explains 1 Sam 21:1's "alone" as alone before the priest, while servants left behind shared the showbread.

pd_work.resource: John Gill, Exposition of the Entire Bible (1746-63), on Matthew 12:3 and Mark 2:26
pd_work.author: John Gill
pd_work.note: Gill treats this exact tension on the row, naming the "he came alone to Ahimelech" objection and answering it from 1 Sam 21:2 (servants left behind); Haley's coverage of this specific alone-vs-companions point is unconfirmed.

link.note: No allowlisted page treats the specific alone-vs-companions tension; the gotquestions.org showbread page addresses only the lawfulness of David eating it, not whether he was alone, so no link is asserted.
